Why laboratory safety and quality matter

Many healthcare decisions are based on medical laboratory test information, so inappropriate laboratory services can harm the patient in several ways.

  • Misdiagnosis.
  • Improper treatment and follow-up, leading to disease progress and adverse events.
  • Improper diagnosis of highly infectious disease cases, which helps to disseminate infection in the surrounding population.

A quality laboratory service is:

  • Safe
  • Effective
  • Patient-centered
  • Efficient
  • Equitable
High-yield

Safety is a component and a result of good quality health service.

Requirements of good quality laboratory services covered in this lesson: accurate identification, effective communication among caregivers, and reduction of healthcare-associated infection (HAI) risk.

Patient and specimen identification

The first requirement is to improve the accuracy of patient and specimen identification at specimen collection, analysis and result delivery.

Patient identification

It must be conducted before:

Performing a diagnostic test
Obtaining blood and other specimens
Giving results

Specimen identification

Label containers used for blood and other specimens in the presence of the patient and fill in a request form. Any specimen with an insufficient label should be rejected.

Do and don't

Do

  • Use at least two patient identifiers
  • Check again with the patient that all details are correct
  • Collect samples from one patient at a time
  • Label specimens straight away, before leaving the patient

Don't

  • Read the patient's details to them and let them passively agree
  • Perform two tasks at the same time (for example, taking samples from several patients and labelling them afterwards)
  • Label a sample bottle before taking the sample, as you may be distracted before completing the task

Acceptable versus unacceptable identifiers

Acceptable

  • Full name (first and last)
  • Date of birth
  • Assigned identification number
  • Telephone number
  • Address
  • Photo ID

Unacceptable

  • Accession number
  • Room number or physical location
  • Diagnosis
  • Procedure

Bar-coding technology

A bar code is a machine-readable code in the form of numbers and a pattern of parallel lines of varying width. It is used as part of the patient identification system as well as the specimen labeling system.

High-yield

Failure to correctly identify patients leads to testing error, diagnosis error, medication error and procedures error.

Communication and healthcare-associated infections

Communication among caregivers

The second requirement is to improve the effectiveness of communication among caregivers, for example communicating life-threatening or life-altering information to the treating physician.

Reducing the risk of HAIs

Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are a patient safety issue affecting all types of health care organizations. One of the most important ways to address them is improving the hand hygiene of health care staff.

An organization should assess its compliance with the CDC and/or WHO guidelines through a comprehensive program that:

  • Provides a hand hygiene policy
  • Fosters a culture of hand hygiene
  • Monitors compliance and provides feedback

Aseptic technique when preparing injections

Rule 1: know what is what

  • Know what is sterile, disinfected and clean.
  • Know what is NOT sterile, not disinfected and not clean.
  • Know how to keep these two categories apart.

Rule 2: ANTT

The critical components are to:

  • Always perform hand hygiene effectively.
  • Never contaminate key parts.
  • Touch non-key parts with confidence.
  • Take appropriate anti-infection precautions.

A non-touch technique is the skill of identifying key-parts and not touching them directly or indirectly. It is vital for achieving asepsis, because the safest way to protect a key-part is simply not to touch it.

Key-part (active)

  • Critical parts of the procedure equipment that come into contact with key-sites
  • If contaminated, they give pathogens a direct route onto or into the patient
  • Examples: needles, syringe tips, IV line connections, lumens, contents of sterile packaging

Key-site

  • Open wounds, including insertion and puncture sites

Important points

  • Do not allow the needle to touch any contaminated surface.
  • Do not reuse a syringe, even if the needle is changed.
  • Do not touch the diaphragm after disinfection with 60-70% alcohol (isopropyl alcohol or ethanol).
  • Do not enter several multidose vials with the same needle and syringe.
  • Do not re-enter a vial with a needle or syringe used on a patient if that vial will be used to withdraw medication again, whether for the same patient or another one.

Sharp exposure

Sharp exposure is handled through preventive measures and post-exposure measures.

Reporting of sharp injury

At a minimum, the log must contain, for each incident, the type and brand of device involved, the department or area of the incident, and a description of the incident.

Post-exposure management

  1. Wound care (first aid)

    Clean wounds with soap and water, and flush mucous membranes with water. Avoid the use of bleach and other agents.

  2. The exposure report

    Record the date and time of exposure, the procedure details (what, where, how, with what device), the exposure details (route, body substance involved, volume or duration of contact), and information about the source person and the exposed person.

  3. Assessment of infection risk

    Assess the source person, the exposed health care worker, and the risk of secondary transmission.

Don't confuse

There is no evidence of benefit for applying antiseptics or disinfectants to the wound, or for squeezing ("milking") puncture sites.

Check yourself

Which two kinds of numbers or places are unacceptable as patient identifiers?

The accession number and the room number or physical location. Diagnosis and procedure are also unacceptable.

When should a specimen container be labelled?

Straight away, in the presence of the patient and before leaving them, never before the sample is taken.

What is the first-aid step for a sharp injury wound?

Clean the wound with soap and water, and flush mucous membranes with water. Do not use bleach or squeeze the puncture site.

Key Points / Quick Review

Quality and safety

  • Quality service is safe, effective, patient-centered, efficient and equitable.
  • Safety is a component and a result of good quality health service.
  • Requirements: accurate identification, communication among caregivers, reduced HAI risk.

Identification

  • Identify the patient before a test, before taking specimens and before giving results.
  • Use at least two identifiers; label in the patient's presence, straight away.
  • Accession number, room number, diagnosis and procedure are unacceptable identifiers.

Aseptic technique

  • ANTT: hand hygiene, protect key parts, touch non-key parts with confidence, take precautions.
  • Never reuse a syringe, even if the needle is changed.
  • Never re-enter a vial with a used needle or syringe if the vial will be reused.

Sharp exposure

  • First aid: soap and water; flush mucous membranes with water.
  • Report the incident, then assess infection risk.
  • Source incidence: HBsAg 30%, HCV antibody 3%, HIV antibody 0.3%.
